summary: Describes Network-Assisted Dynamic Adaptation, an experimental congestion control scheme for interactive real-time media like video conferencing. The sender adjusts its rate from implicit or explicit congestion signals and can use ECN marks from the network, behaving consistently when marks are absent.

The receiver measures how much delay, packet loss and congestion marking the traffic is suffering, turns that into one number, and sends it back. The sender then speeds up or slows down according to that number, and it behaves the same way whichever signals the network happens to provide.

subtitle: A congestion control scheme for real-time media that reads delay, loss and explicit marking as one signal.

tldr.problem: Real-time media needs a congestion control scheme that reacts quickly to bandwidth changes, tolerates a fluctuating video encoder, keeps queuing delay low, and makes use of every available congestion signal at once.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver combines measured queuing delay, ECN markings and packet loss into a single number, an equivalent delay, and sends it back with the rate mode and the receiving rate in a 48-bit RTCP feedback message.
tldr.outcome: The sender either ramps up multiplicatively while the path is underused or adjusts the rate gradually in proportion to the signal, and the resulting rates are proportional to each flow's priority when several share a bottleneck.

today: RFC 8698 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document reports implementations in the ns-2 and ns-3 simulators, an open-source ns-3 module, and a reference implementation built by modifying the WebRTC module of the Mozilla browser, and it asks for further experiments in real-world settings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Interactive real-time media applications introduce a unique set of challenges for congestion control. Unlike TCP, the mechanism used for real-time media needs to adapt quickly to instantaneous bandwidth changes, accommodate fluctuations in the output of video encoder rate control, and cause low queuing delay over the network. An ideal scheme should also make effective use of all types of congestion signals, including packet loss, queuing delay and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) markings (RFC 3168).

The requirements for the algorithm are outlined in the RMCAT congestion control requirements. They highlight that the desired scheme should avoid flow starvation and attain a reasonable fair share of bandwidth when competing against other flows, adapt quickly, and operate in a stable manner.

This document describes an experimental congestion control scheme called Network-Assisted Dynamic Adaptation (NADA). The design benefits from explicit congestion control signals such as ECN markings from the network, yet also operates when only implicit congestion indicators, that is delay and or loss, are available. That unified sender behaviour distinguishes NADA from other congestion control schemes for real-time media. Its core algorithm is designed to guarantee stability for path round-trip times below a prescribed bound, for example 250 ms with the default parameter choices, and it supports weighted bandwidth sharing among competing video flows with different priorities.

The signalling mechanism consists of standard Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) timestamps (RFC 3550) and RTCP feedback reports. The definition of the desired RTCP feedback message is described in the related RTCP feedback draft, so as to support the successful operation of several congestion control schemes for real-time interactive media.
sections.plainLanguage: NADA is a way for a video sender to decide how fast to send. The receiver measures how much delay, packet loss and congestion marking the traffic is suffering, turns that into one number, and sends it back. The sender then speeds up or slows down according to that number, and it behaves the same way whichever signals the network happens to provide.

sections.title: System Overview
sections.content:
The system has four parts. The media encoder with rate control capabilities encodes raw media frames into a compressed bitstream that is later packetized into RTP packets. Its actual output rate may fluctuate around the target rate, and it may only be able to react to bit rate changes at coarse intervals, for example once every 0.5 seconds.

The RTP sender calculates the NADA reference rate from network congestion indicators, that is delay, loss or ECN marking reports from the receiver; updates the video encoder with a new target rate; and regulates the actual sending rate accordingly. It also generates a sending timestamp for each outgoing packet.

The RTP receiver measures and estimates end-to-end delay from the sender timestamp, packet loss from the RTP sequence numbers, ECN marking ratios, and the receiving rate of the flow. It calculates the aggregated congestion signal, which accounts for queuing delay, ECN markings and packet losses, and determines the mode for sender rate adaptation based on whether the flow has encountered any standing non-zero congestion. It sends periodic RTCP reports back to the sender containing the aggregated signal, the mode and the receiving rate.

The network node may work with the default behaviour of a simple drop-tail queue, and can also benefit from advanced Active Queue Management features such as PIE (RFC 8033), FQ-CoDel (RFC 8290), ECN marking based on Random Early Detection (RFC 7567), and Pre-Congestion Notification marking using a token bucket algorithm (RFC 6660). Network node operation is out of scope for the design of NADA.
sections.plainLanguage: The encoder makes video and hands it to the sender, which packetizes it and sends it into the network. The receiver measures what the traffic experienced, turns it into a single congestion number, and sends that number back in a periodic report. The sender uses it to set a new rate for the encoder and for the packets on the wire.

sections.title: The Receiver-Side Algorithm
sections.content:
On initialization the receiver sets the baseline delay to positive infinity, the loss and marking ratios to zero and the receiving rate to zero. On every media packet it takes the current timestamp, reads the sending timestamp from the packet header, and computes the one-way delay as the difference between them. It updates the baseline delay as the minimum of the baseline and this delay, computes the queuing delay as the difference between the one-way delay and the baseline, and updates the loss ratio, the marking ratio and the receiving rate.

When it is time to send a new feedback report, the receiver calculates the non-linear warping of the delay if packet loss exists, calculates the current aggregated congestion signal, determines the mode of rate adaptation for the sender, and sends a feedback message containing the mode, the signal and the receiving rate.

It matters to distinguish levels of observed queuing delay. Over wired connections a moderate queuing delay on the order of tens of milliseconds is likely self-inflicted or induced by other delay-based flows, whereas a high queuing delay of several hundred milliseconds may indicate the presence of a loss-based flow that does not refrain from increased delay. So if the last observed packet loss is within the expiration window, the estimated queuing delay follows a non-linear warping: the value is unchanged when it is below the threshold QTH, and is otherwise scaled down along a non-linear curve. This warping is inspired by a delay-adaptive congestion window backoff policy, so as to gradually nudge the controller to operate on loss-induced congestion signals when competing against loss-based flows. The threshold should be tuned for the environment, with a higher value needed in a noisier one such as a wireless connection, and the document says further studies should gather insight on how to tune or auto-tune it.

The expiration window self-scales with the average packet loss interval using a multiplier, following the estimation method in the TFRC specification. In practice it is recommended to linearly interpolate between the warped and non-warped values of the queuing delay during the transitional period lasting for the duration of that interval.

The aggregated congestion signal is the warped queuing delay plus a delay penalty for ECN markings scaled by the square of the marking ratio over the reference marking ratio, and a delay penalty for losses scaled by the square of the loss ratio over the reference loss ratio. The penalties do not depend on the configuration at the network node. Since ECN-enabled queue management schemes typically mark a packet before dropping it, the loss penalty SHOULD be higher than the marking penalty, and the two values need to be set consistently across all NADA flows sharing the same bottleneck link so that they compete fairly. In the absence of markings and losses, the signal reduces to the observed queuing delay, and NADA operates as a delay-based scheme.

The receiver also decides the mode. Accelerated ramp-up is used when there have been no recent packet losses within the observation window and no buildup of queuing delay, that is when the difference between the one-way delay and the baseline stayed below the queue threshold for all previous delay samples in the window. Otherwise the algorithm operates in gradual update mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver turns three different problems into one number. Delay above the path's own minimum is queuing delay. Loss and congestion marking are each converted into an equivalent number of milliseconds of delay and added on. If the last loss was recent, the queuing delay is scaled down so that the sender does not ignore congestion just because a competing TCP connection is filling the queue.

sections.title: The Sender-Side Algorithm
sections.content:
On initialization the sender sets the reference rate to the minimum rate, the round-trip time estimate to zero and the previous congestion signal to zero. On each feedback report it reads the mode, the signal and the receiving rate, updates its round-trip time estimate, measures the interval since the last report, and updates the reference rate either by the accelerated ramp-up rules or the gradual update rules, depending on the mode. The rate is then clipped to the range between the minimum and maximum rates.

In accelerated ramp-up mode, the rate increase multiplier is the smaller of a maximum value and the ratio of the upper bound on self-inflicted queuing delay to the round-trip time plus the target feedback interval and the bound on filtering delay. The reference rate is then set to the larger of its previous value and one plus the multiplier times the receiving rate. The rationale is that the longer it takes the sender to observe self-inflicted queuing delay buildup, the more conservative the sender should be in increasing its rate, and hence the smaller the multiplier.

In gradual update mode the rate changes in proportion to the previous rate decision. It is affected by two terms: the offset of the aggregated congestion signal from its value at equilibrium, and the change in the signal since the last report. The offset depends on the maximum rate of the flow, its weight of priority and a reference congestion signal. The reference value is chosen so that the maximum rate can be achieved when the observed congestion signal is below priority times that reference.

At equilibrium the aggregated signal stabilizes at priority times the reference congestion level times the maximum rate divided by the reference rate. This ensures that when several flows share the same bottleneck and observe a common signal value, their rates at equilibrium are proportional to their respective priority levels and the range between minimum and maximum rate. The minimum and maximum rates come from the media codec, and in the absence of that information the sender chooses a default minimum of 0 and a default maximum of 3 Mbps.
sections.plainLanguage: While the path looks underused, the sender raises its rate by a factor, but by less when the round trip is long, so it does not create its own delay. Once there is a congestion signal, the sender adjusts the rate in proportion to how far the signal is above its equilibrium value and how fast that value is changing. Because the equilibrium depends on the flow's priority, flows sharing a bottleneck settle at rates in proportion to their priorities.

sections.title: The Feedback Message
sections.content:
Three pieces of information are needed for NADA congestion control to function properly. The recommended rate adaptation mode is a 1-bit flag saying whether the sender should operate in accelerated ramp-up mode or in gradual update mode. The aggregated congestion signal is the most recently updated value calculated by the receiver; it can be expressed with a unit of 100 microseconds, that is one tenth of a millisecond, in 15 bits, which allows a maximum value of the signal at approximately 3.27 seconds. The receiving rate is the most recently measured receiving rate; it is expressed in bits per second in 32 bits as an unsigned integer, allowing a maximum rate of approximately 4.3 Gbps, roughly 1000 times the streaming rate of a typical high-definition video conferencing session.

Together these fit in 48 bits, or 6 bytes. They can be included in the feedback report from the receiver, or, in the case where all receiver-side calculations are moved to the sender, derived from per-packet information in the feedback message defined in the related RTCP feedback draft. A target feedback interval of 100 ms is recommended.

On the choice of interval, the document notes that it has to balance timely feedback against a low count of feedback messages. An interval of 100 ms corresponds to a feedback bandwidth of 16 Kbps with 200 bytes per feedback message, about 1.6 percent overhead for a 1 Mbps flow. Both simulation studies and frequency-domain analysis have established that an interval below 250 ms, that is more frequently than four feedback messages per second, will not break up the feedback control loop of NADA.
sections.plainLanguage: The report the receiver sends back has three fields and fits in six bytes: one bit saying which mode the sender should use, a 15-bit congestion number measured in tenths of a millisecond, and a 32-bit receiving rate in bits per second. Sending it ten times a second costs about 1.6 percent of the flow at 1 Mbps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The rate adaptation mechanism in NADA relies on feedback from the receiver, so it is vulnerable to attacks where feedback messages are hijacked, replaced, or intentionally injected with misleading information, resulting in denial of service, similar to those that can affect TCP. It is therefore RECOMMENDED that the RTCP feedback message is at least integrity checked. The related RTCP feedback draft discusses the potential risk of a receiver providing misleading congestion feedback information and the mechanisms for mitigating those risks.

The modification of the sending rate based on the sender-side rate-shaping buffer may lead to temporary excessive congestion over the network in the presence of an unresponsive video encoder. This effect can be mitigated by limiting the amount of rate modification introduced by the buffer, bounding the size of the buffer at the sender, and maintaining a maximum allowed sending rate by NADA.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender trusts what the receiver reports, so an attacker who can alter those reports can make the sender flood the network or stop sending. The feedback message should therefore be checked for tampering.

messages.label: ENCODED MEDIA
messages.note: Compressed frames at the encoder's output rate.

messages.label: RTP PACKETS
messages.note: Sent at the regulated sending rate, each with a timestamp.

messages.label: ARRIVING PACKETS
messages.note: Delayed, and possibly marked or dropped along the way.

messages.label: RTCP FEEDBACK REPORT
messages.note: Carries the rate mode, the aggregated congestion signal and the receiving rate.

fields.name: rmode
fields.desc: Rate update mode: 0 for accelerated ramp up, 1 for gradual update.

fields.name: x_curr
fields.desc: Aggregated congestion signal, in units of 100 microseconds. Maximum about 3.27 seconds.

fields.name: r_recv
fields.desc: Receiving rate in bits per second, unsigned. Maximum about 4.3 Gbps.

items.title: Accelerated ramp up
items.text: Used when the path looks underused. The rate rises by a factor, limited so the sender does not create its own queuing delay.

items.title: Gradual update
items.text: Used once there is a congestion signal. The rate changes in proportion to how far the signal is above its equilibrium value, and how fast it is moving.
